prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Statistical modeling of experimental physical laws is based on the probability density function of measured variables. It is expressed by experimental data via a kernel estimator. The kernel is determined objectively by the scattering of data during calibration of experimental setup. A physical law, which relates measured variables, is optimally extracted from experimental data by the conditional average estimator. It is derived directly from the kernel estimator and corresponds to a general nonparametric regression. The proposed method is demonstrated by the modeling of a return map of noisy chaotic data. In this example, the nonparametric regression is used to predict a future value of chaotic time series from the present one. The mean predictor error is used in the definition of predictor quality, while the redundancy is expressed by the mean square distance between data points. Both statistics are used in a new definition of predictor cost function. From the minimum of the predictor cost function, a proper number of data in the model is estimated.

Statistical modeling of experimental physical laws is based on the probability density function of measured variables, which is represented from experimental data using a kernel estimator. The kernel is determined objectively from the scatter observed during calibration of the experimental setup. A physical law relating the measured variables is optimally extracted from the experimental data using a conditional average estimator. Derived directly from the kernel estimator, this approach corresponds to a general nonparametric regression.

The proposed method is demonstrated by modeling a return map of noisy chaotic data. The mean prediction error is used to define predictor quality, while redundancy is quantified by the mean squared distance between data points. Both statistics are incorporated into a new definition of the predictor cost function. The appropriate number of data points to include in the model is then estimated from the minimum of this cost function.

The kernel is selected objectively according to the amount of data scatter observed during calibration of the experimental apparatus. The physical relationship among the measured variables is then recovered optimally through a conditional-mean estimator. Because this estimator follows directly from the kernel density estimate, it constitutes a general form of nonparametric regression.

The method is illustrated by constructing a return map from noisy chaotic observations. In this case, nonparametric regression predicts the next value of a chaotic time series from its current value. Predictor quality is defined using the mean prediction error, whereas redundancy is quantified by the mean squared distance between data points. outputs.L3:
Statistical modeling of experimental physical laws can be based directly on the probability density function of the measured variables. Rather than assuming a predefined functional form, this density is estimated from the observed data using a kernel estimator. The kernel and its bandwidth are selected objectively from the degree of data scattering measured during calibration of the experimental setup, thereby incorporating experimental uncertainty into the statistical description.

Once the joint probability distribution of the relevant variables has been estimated, the physical relationship between them can be extracted through a conditional average estimator. This approach provides a general form of nonparametric regression: it identifies the expected value of one variable conditioned on the observed values of others without requiring an explicit analytical model in advance.

The method can be illustrated by predicting future values of a noisy chaotic time series from its present values. A return map is constructed to describe the relationship between the current state and a subsequent state, while kernel-based conditional averaging yields the corresponding predictor despite noise and irregular dynamics.

To determine how much data should be used, a predictor cost function is introduced. This function balances two competing effects: the mean prediction error, which generally decreases as more information is included, and data redundancy, which increases when additional observations contribute little independent information. The minimum of this cost function identifies the appropriate amount of data needed to build an accurate, efficient, and nonredundant model.
outputs.L4:
The study presents an objective, nonparametric approach for identifying physical laws directly from experimental data. Rather than assuming a predetermined functional form for the underlying dynamics, the method represents relationships among measured variables through probability densities estimated with kernel techniques. These density estimates are then used to construct a regression model capable of approximating the evolution law of the observed system.

The approach is applied to the prediction of noisy data generated by a chaotic return map. A central challenge is determining how many past observations should be included in the predictor. Too few observations may omit information needed to describe the dynamics, whereas too many can introduce redundant variables, increase estimation uncertainty, and reduce predictive performance.

To address this problem, the study defines a cost function that balances two competing factors: the mean prediction error and the redundancy among the observations used by the model. Minimizing this cost provides a data-driven criterion for selecting the appropriate number of inputs. The resulting model captures relevant dynamical information while avoiding unnecessary complexity.

The results show that combining kernel-based regression with this error–redundancy criterion improves both predictor selection and prediction quality for noisy chaotic data. More broadly, the framework offers a flexible way to infer governing relationships from experimental probability distributions without imposing restrictive parametric assumptions.
outputs.L5:
**The Value of Statistical Analysis**

Statistical analysis helps people understand complex information by identifying patterns, trends, and relationships in data. The results can support decisions in fields such as science, business, healthcare, and education. Both accurate data collection and careful interpretation are essential, because even advanced statistical methods can produce misleading conclusions when the underlying information is incomplete or biased. By combining reliable evidence with thoughtful judgment, statistical analysis becomes a powerful tool for solving real-world problems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a research paper on nonparametric statistical modeling of experimental physical laws using kernel density estimation and conditional averaging, with an application to noisy chaotic return maps.
counterfactuals.output: We present a nonparametric framework for identifying statistical physical laws from noisy experimental data. The method estimates the joint probability density of measured input–response variables using kernel density estimation and reconstructs the underlying law through conditional averaging. Unlike parametric regression, the approach requires no prescribed functional form and naturally accommodates nonlinear, multivalued, and heteroscedastic relationships. Bandwidth selection and finite-sample effects are addressed to balance noise suppression against resolution of fine-scale structure. We apply the framework to return maps generated by noisy chaotic systems, where measurement uncertainty and intrinsic fluctuations obscure the deterministic mapping. Conditional means recover the dominant return-map geometry, while conditional variances quantify local departures from deterministic behavior and reveal state-dependent uncertainty. The resulting representation separates systematic dynamics from stochastic variability and provides probabilistic predictions across the reconstructed state space. These results demonstrate that kernel-based conditional averaging offers a flexible and interpretable tool for extracting experimental laws from complex physical data without imposing restrictive model assumptions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how physical relationships can be extracted from noisy experimental data using an objectively calibrated kernel estimator and general nonparametric regression.
counterfactuals.output:
Physical relationships can be extracted from noisy measurements without assuming a specific equation in advance by estimating the conditional mean

\[
m(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid \mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}],
\]

where \(\mathbf{x}\) contains measured physical variables and \(Y\) is the response. A kernel estimator reconstructs this relationship locally, while objective calibration determines how much smoothing is justified by the data.

## 1. Kernel regression

For observations \((\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\), a basic kernel estimate is

\[
\hat m(\mathbf{x})=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_H(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_i)y_i}
     {\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_H(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_i)}.
\]

The kernel \(K_H\) gives greater weight to observations near \(\mathbf{x}\). The bandwidth matrix \(H\) sets the neighborhood size:

- too small: the estimate follows experimental noise;
- too large: genuine physical structure is erased.

Local polynomial regression is often preferable. Near each query point, it fits a low-order polynomial using kernel weights. A local-linear fit, for example, minimizes

\[
\sum_i K_H(\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x})
\left[y_i-a-\mathbf{b}^{T}(\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x})\right]^2.
\]

Here, \(\hat a\) estimates the physical response and \(\hat{\mathbf b}\) estimates its local derivatives. Local-linear methods reduce boundary bias and directly provide slopes such as response coefficients, susceptibilities, or transport gradients.

## 2. Objective calibration

The bandwidth and other tuning parameters should not be chosen by visual preference. They can be calibrated using reproducible criteria such as:

- leave-one-out cross-validation;
- generalized cross-validation;
- unbiased risk estimates;
- likelihood or marginal-likelihood optimization;
- plug-in bandwidth rules;
- validation on independent experiments.

For squared-error cross-validation, one chooses

\[
\hat H=\arg\min_H
\sum_i\left[y_i-\hat m_{-i,H}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right]^2,
\]

where \(\hat m_{-i,H}\) is computed without observation \(i\). If measurement uncertainties \(\sigma_i\) differ, a weighted criterion is more appropriate:

\[
\hat H=\arg\min_H
\sum_i\frac{\left[y_i-\hat m_{-i,H}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right]^2}{\sigma_i^2}.
\]

This makes the smoothing scale an empirical consequence of predictive performance rather than a subjective plotting choice. Nested cross-validation should be used if the same data are also used to assess final predictive accuracy.

## 3. Recovering physical information

Once \(\hat m\) is calibrated, it can reveal:

- monotonic or nonlinear response curves;
- thresholds, saturation, and regime changes;
- interactions among control variables;
- derivatives such as \(\partial m/\partial x_j\);
- extrema and transition locations;
- scaling behavior and dimensionless collapse;
- residual structures indicating omitted variables or missing physics.

For example, a local estimate of

\[
\frac{\partial m}{\partial T}
\]

may represent a temperature coefficient, while a zero crossing of a derivative may identify a critical point. Confidence intervals must accompany these features, especially because differentiation amplifies noise.

## 4. General nonparametric regression

Kernel regression is one member of a broader class that includes splines, Gaussian processes, local polynomials, regression trees, random forests, and neural-network smoothers. These methods estimate

\[
Y=m(\mathbf X)+\varepsilon
\]

with minimal assumptions about the form of \(m\).

Model and hyperparameter selection can again be made objectively by out-of-sample predictive criteria. Agreement among several well-calibrated nonparametric estimators strengthens evidence that a recovered feature is data-supported rather than an artifact of one method.

## 5. Uncertainty and experimental complications

Reliable physical interpretation requires more than a smooth curve:

1. **Estimate uncertainty.** Use bootstrap intervals, asymptotic local-regression errors, or posterior intervals.
2. **Account for correlated observations.** Resample whole runs, specimens, or time blocks rather than individual points.
3. **Treat errors in inputs.** Ordinary kernel regression assumes \(\mathbf{x}\) is measured accurately. Significant input noise requires errors-in-variables, deconvolution, or latent-variable methods.
4. **Handle heteroscedasticity.** Model the conditional variance  
   \[
   v(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathbf X=\mathbf{x})
   \]
   or use uncertainty-weighted fitting.
5. **Avoid unsupported extrapolation.** Nonparametric estimates are generally reliable only where the experiment supplies adequate data density.
6. **Control dimensionality.** With many predictors, use physically motivated variables, dimensionless groups, additive models, or regularization to mitigate the curse of dimensionality.
7. **Respect physical constraints.** Positivity, monotonicity, conservation laws, symmetries, and known boundary conditions can be imposed during estimation.

## 6. From empirical relationship to physical law

A nonparametric fit is not automatically a physical law. It first provides a model-independent map of the relationship supported by the experiment. That map can then be used to:

1. identify robust trends and regimes;
2. propose a simpler mechanistic equation;
3. estimate its parameters;
4. compare its predictions with the nonparametric benchmark;
5. test it on new experiments.

Thus, the objectively calibrated kernel estimator acts as a low-assumption discovery tool. It separates reproducible structure from noise, quantifies uncertainty, and supplies evidence from which interpretable physical models can be formulated and tested.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output: The method reconstructs the state space of a chaotic time series from present and lagged observations, then predicts future values using nearby historical states and their subsequent evolution. counterfactuals.prompt: Propose a data-driven framework for modeling experimental physical laws based on probability density functions, kernel estimation, conditional averages, and a predictor cost function.
counterfactuals.output:
## Probability-Density Framework for Data-Driven Physical Laws

Consider experimental observations

\[
\mathcal D=\{(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf y_i)\}_{i=1}^{N},
\]

where \(\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d\) contains measured state or control variables and \(\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^m\) contains responses such as force, flux, acceleration, or reaction rate. A physical law is represented statistically by the joint probability density

\[
p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y),
\]

rather than being restricted a priori to a particular algebraic form.

### 1. Estimate the experimental probability density

Use kernel density estimation (KDE):

\[
\widehat p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
K_{\mathbf H_x}(\mathbf x-\mathbf x_i)
K_{\mathbf H_y}(\mathbf y-\mathbf y_i),
\]

where \(K\) is a normalized kernel and \(\mathbf H_x,\mathbf H_y\) are bandwidth matrices. For Gaussian kernels,

\[
K_{\mathbf H}(\mathbf z)
=
\frac{
\exp[-\tfrac12\mathbf z^\top\mathbf H^{-1}\mathbf z]
}{
(2\pi)^{d/2}|\mathbf H|^{1/2}
}.
\]

Bandwidths can be selected by cross-validation or likelihood maximization and should account for measurement uncertainty and differing physical scales.

The marginal and conditional densities are

\[
\widehat p(\mathbf x)=\int \widehat p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y,
\qquad
\widehat p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x)
=
\frac{\widehat p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)}
{\widehat p(\mathbf x)}.
\]

Thus the framework provides both a constitutive prediction and its experimental uncertainty.

### 2. Define the physical law as a conditional average

For squared prediction error, the data-driven law is the conditional mean

\[
\widehat{\mathbf f}(\mathbf x)
=
\mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X=\mathbf x]
=
\int \mathbf y\,\widehat p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf y.
\]

With a product KDE, this becomes the Nadaraya–Watson estimator

\[
\widehat{\mathbf f}(\mathbf x)
=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
K_{\mathbf H_x}(\mathbf x-\mathbf x_i)\mathbf y_i
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
K_{\mathbf H_x}(\mathbf x-\mathbf x_i)
}.
\]

Hence nearby experiments contribute more strongly than distant ones, without imposing a polynomial, power law, or neural-network architecture.

Conditional fluctuations characterize unresolved variables and experimental noise:

\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}(\mathbf x)
=
\mathbb E\!\left[
(\mathbf Y-\widehat{\mathbf f})
(\mathbf Y-\widehat{\mathbf f})^\top
\mid \mathbf X=\mathbf x
\right].
\]

Prediction intervals or probabilistic forecasts should be obtained from the full conditional density, especially when it is skewed or multimodal.

### 3. Derive the predictor from a cost function

Let \(\mathbf g(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) be a candidate physical-law predictor. Define its population cost as

\[
\mathcal C[\mathbf g]
=
\iint
L\!\left(\mathbf y,\mathbf g(\mathbf x)\right)
p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf x\,d\mathbf y.
\]

For a weighted quadratic loss,

\[
L(\mathbf y,\mathbf g)
=
(\mathbf y-\mathbf g)^\top
\mathbf W(\mathbf x)
(\mathbf y-\mathbf g),
\]

the unconstrained minimizer satisfies

\[
\mathbf g^*(\mathbf x)=\mathbb E[\mathbf Y\mid\mathbf X=\mathbf x].
\]

The empirical KDE-based cost is

\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\iint
L\!\left(\mathbf y,\mathbf g(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\theta)\right)
\widehat p(\mathbf x,\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf x\,d\mathbf y.
\]

A practical approximation is the cross-validated risk

\[
\widehat{\mathcal C}_{\rm CV}(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
L\!\left(
\mathbf y_i,
\mathbf g_{-i}(\mathbf x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)
\right),
\]

where \(\mathbf g_{-i}\) is fitted without sample \(i\). This avoids overly narrow bandwidths and overfitting.

Other losses define different statistical laws:

- absolute loss \(\rightarrow\) conditional median;
- quantile loss \(\rightarrow\) conditional quantiles;
- negative log-likelihood \(\rightarrow\) full conditional-density prediction;
- robust Huber loss \(\rightarrow\) reduced sensitivity to outliers.

### 4. Incorporate physical structure

Known physical information can be introduced through constrained model classes or penalties:

\[
\mathcal C_{\rm phys}[\mathbf g]
=
\widehat{\mathcal C}[\mathbf g]
+
\lambda_R\mathcal R[\mathbf g]
+
\sum_k \lambda_k\mathcal P_k[\mathbf g].
\]

Possible terms include:

- dimensional consistency and nondimensional variables;
- conservation laws;
- rotational, translational, or permutation symmetries;
- positivity and boundedness;
- monotonicity or convexity;
- smoothness, such as
  \[
  \mathcal R[\mathbf g]=\int \|\nabla^2\mathbf g(\mathbf x)\|^2p(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x;
  \]
- thermodynamic restrictions such as nonnegative dissipation.

Hard constraints may be built into \(\mathbf g\); uncertain principles are better represented as soft penalties.

### 5. Validation and law extraction

A complete workflow is:

1. Nondimensionalize variables and quantify measurement errors.
2. Estimate the joint or conditional density using KDE.
3. Select bandwidths using blocked or leave-one-experiment-out validation.
4. Compute conditional means, variances, and quantiles.
5. Fit an interpretable predictor \(\mathbf g(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\theta)\) by minimizing the density-weighted cost.
6. Enforce known physical constraints.
7. Validate on independent experimental regimes.
8. Detect extrapolation using the estimated support:
   \[
   \widehat p(\mathbf x)<\varepsilon
   \quad\Rightarrow\quad
   \text{prediction flagged as unsupported}.
   \]

If a compact symbolic law is desired, candidate formulas can be fitted to the nonparametric conditional mean using

\[
\min_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\int
\left\|
\widehat{\mathbf f}(\mathbf x)
-
\mathbf g(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\theta)
\right\|^2
\widehat p(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x
+
\lambda\,\mathrm{Complexity}(\mathbf g).
\]

This separates two tasks: the density estimate captures what the experiments imply, while the constrained predictor provides a compact, interpretable physical law.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study in which kernel-based nonparametric regression is applied to noisy chaotic data, including how predictor quality, data-point redundancy, and optimal sample size are defined.
counterfactuals.output:
The study treats prediction of a noisy chaotic time series as a nonparametric regression problem. Delay-coordinate vectors are formed from past observations, and a future value is estimated by a kernel-weighted average of the futures associated with nearby vectors:

\[
\hat{x}_{t+\tau}=
\frac{\sum_i K\!\left(\|X_t-X_i\|/h\right)x_{i+\tau}}
     {\sum_i K\!\left(\|X_t-X_i\|/h\right)} ,
\]

where \(h\) is the kernel bandwidth. Tests on simulated chaotic systems with added observational noise show the usual bias–variance trade-off: narrow kernels follow local deterministic structure but are sensitive to noise and sparse sampling, whereas wide kernels suppress noise but smooth away nonlinear detail.

The paper uses three related operational concepts:

- **Predictor quality:** out-of-sample agreement between predicted and true future values, measured by normalized prediction error—equivalently, a skill score such as  
  \[
  Q=1-\frac{\langle(x-\hat x)^2\rangle}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}.
  \]
  Thus \(Q=1\) denotes perfect prediction and \(Q\approx0\) denotes performance comparable to predicting the mean. Some results may be reported as normalized RMSE or correlation, but the principle is independent-test predictive skill.

- **Data-point redundancy:** a training point is redundant when it adds essentially no new local information—its kernel neighborhood is already represented by other, nearby observations, so removing it causes negligible change in the fitted predictor or its test error. Redundancy therefore reflects overlap in reconstructed state space, not merely repeated scalar values.

- **Optimal sample size:** the number of retained training points that maximizes cross-validated predictor quality, or, when performance has plateaued, the smallest sample giving statistically indistinguishable maximum quality. Beyond this size, extra points are mostly redundant and increase computational cost without meaningful predictive gain.

The main conclusion is that, for noisy chaotic data, prediction depends more on effective coverage of the reconstructed attractor than on the raw record length. Kernel bandwidth, noise level, embedding dimension, and sampling density jointly determine how many observations are genuinely informative; consequently, a carefully selected subset can predict nearly as well as—or occasionally better than—the full, highly redundant data set.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
